item.title: Papoose Accuses Eazy The Block Captain Of Betrayal On “Handshakes With Snakes”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Papoose accused Eazy The Block Captain of betrayal on "Handshakes With Snakes" after "Letter To Claressa" reached YouTube.
item.content:encoded:
Papoose accused Eazy The Block Captain of betraying his trust on “Handshakes With Snakes.” The new diss brought their old fight and his split from Remy Ma back into the booth.

The Ron Browz-produced track reached Papoose’s official YouTube channel Friday, October 30, at about 5:57 P.M. Eastern. Earlier that day, at about 6:18 A.M., Eazy released “Letter To Claressa”, directing his attack on Papoose toward the rapper’s partner, boxer Claressa Shields.

Pap returned to his claim that he knocked Eazy unconscious during their past confrontation. Eazy has repeatedly disputed that account. He acknowledged getting punched but denied being knocked out, a distinction that has followed this feud for years.

On the new record, Papoose also accused Eazy of repeating false stories about his private life. His attack tied Eazy’s past romance with Remy to what he described as a breach of trust after the two men had been friendly.

Eazy took a different route on his record. Addressing Shields as if he were writing her a letter, he questioned Papoose’s intentions and portrayed the rapper as dependent on her money. He urged her to leave the relationship and focus on her own career.

Both songs followed an already busy stretch of exchanges. Eazy released “Lothario” on October 10, bringing Shields and Papoose’s marriage into the dispute. AllHipHop then covered Papoose’s “Food For Thought” freestyle on October 27. That performance also included his disputed knockout claim.

The personal history helps explain why each man’s new song reached beyond the other rapper. Rumors linking Remy and Eazy circulated after the June 2023 confrontation at a Chrome 23 event. Remy also denied that Papoose knocked Eazy out.

In December 2024, the conflict became a public argument over both relationships. Remy posted what she said were private messages between Papoose and Shields. Papoose accused Remy of cheating, while Shields accused her of having other relationships. Shields later said her private romance with Papoose began in August 2024.

Eazy gave his own account during a December 12, 2024 livestream. He acknowledged a two-year relationship with Remy and claimed she and Papoose had already separated. Their differing versions of when the marriage broke down remained central to the argument.

Remy made her feelings for Eazy public at Chrome 23’s “Read The Room” event in January 2025. During his battle with Shotgun Suge, she answered yes when Eazy asked whether she loved him.

The music carried the dispute through this year. Remy challenged Papoose’s claims about writing her rhymes on “W.Y.F.L.” in April. His September record “Jezebel” repeated infidelity and writing claims amid another public clash between Remy and Shields. Remy followed with the EP Alimony and “Why I Get Married?” featuring Keke Wyatt on September 25.

For Papoose, the newest record’s closing image was a handshake. He built an extended passage around what he felt Eazy owed him after being welcomed around his family, turning each finger into part of the trust he accused the battle rapper of breaking.

item.title: 50 Cent Taunts Tia Kemp After She Says She Can’t Go Live
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: 50 Cent reposted Tia Kemp's complaint about losing Instagram Live access as their dispute continued ahead of a November 3 hearing.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent reposted Tia Kemp’s Instagram complaint that she could no longer go Live. The new post extended a feud that has led to a lawsuit and an order protecting his teenage son.

“I can’t go Live,” Kemp wrote in the Story, followed by laughing faces and three rat emojis. She also urged people to stop reporting her.

The rat emojis appeared to suggest someone had snitched, but the post offered no proof that 50 caused her reported restriction. It also did not include an explanation from Instagram about the reason she could no longer use the Live feature.

He shared the complaint with Jermaine Jackson’s “Don’t Take It Personal” and added his own caption: “Street Fighter in theaters now !”

The repost put Kemp’s frustration back in front of his audience after a series of increasingly personal exchanges.

She is the mother of Rick Ross’ son William Roberts III, whose reported assault helped set off this round of the argument.

According to Daytona Beach police, Roberts, a Bethune-Cookman football player, reported an October 11 assault. Police said he was talking to a woman when the suspect pointed a handgun at him and struck him.

Don Roberts III was arrested on aggravated assault and aggravated battery charges involving a deadly weapon.

50 later offered to help the accused man with bond and shared his denial of wrongdoing. “I had a strong feeling this brother was innocent,” he wrote on Instagram.

Kemp objected to 50’s involvement in the situation, telling him, “U have NO room to post anyone’s child” after he posted about her son.

That conflict also produced a separate California federal lawsuit in which 50 sought $6 million.

His complaint accused Kemp of inventing a developmental diagnosis for his son Sire and making degrading claims about Sire’s mother, Daphne Joy.

Kemp also made a mock GoFundMe appeal over the $6 million demand, turning the lawsuit into another subject for her online jokes.

A temporary Florida restraining order issued October 26 protected Sire, 14. It required Kemp to remain 500 feet away and barred direct or indirect contact, including through social media.

The court set a November 3 hearing on a longer injunction.

item.title: Jack Harlow Previews New Music Alongside Babyface After R&B Turn
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Jack Harlow previewed new music alongside Babyface after taking his sound toward R&B on his fourth album, *Monica*.
item.content:encoded:
Jack Harlow previewed new music alongside Babyface, putting the rapper next to an R&B veteran after he traded rap verses for singing on Monica.

The singer, songwriter and producer has remained part of R&B’s current sound and its history. His work on SZA’s “Snooze” earned him a Grammy for Best R&B Song in 2024.

For Harlow, the preview followed a much broader change in how he made music. His fourth album, Monica, arrived March 13 with songs built around love and relationships. He recorded it at Electric Lady Studios in New York’s Greenwich Village after moving from Kentucky to New York City.

Harlow had explained his shift toward R&B on “Popcast,” where he talked about setting aside some of the habits that came with rapping.

“Part of the reason I love rap music is the braggadocio of it,” he said.

He wanted to find a way to write with less boasting. That meant changing the rules before he got to the microphone: no rapping and no cursing. He also ruled out digital instruments apart from drums, requiring the other instruments to be played live.

Those limits were meant to challenge his writing and stop him from relying on familiar shortcuts. His listening had changed, too. After the move to New York, softer, more melodic music helped shape what he wanted to make.

The album also brought in musicians from across R&B and jazz. Ravyn Lenae contributed vocals to “Prague,” “My Winter,” and “All Of My Friends.”

Jermaine Paul and Omar Apollo also contributed vocals, while Robert Glasper played piano on the closing song, “Say Hello.”

That approach carried into his live sets. He had signaled the ambition behind the change well before the album arrived.

“I’m trying to transcend,” Harlow told Apple Music in March 2025. On the time needed to make something different, he said, “I’m just slowly starting to accept that it is going to take me longer than any of my past projects.”

item.title: Kevin Gates Shrugs Off Dreka’s $1M-Plus Catalog Order
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kevin Gates said he had no hard feelings over sharing catalog proceeds with Dreka and discussed what his children taught him.
item.content:encoded:
Kevin Gates said he had no hard feelings about sharing proceeds from his music catalog with estranged wife Dreka Gates, saying he had given far more to people he loved.

On “The TMZ Podcast” this week, Gates compared a portion of the sale money with the whole world he said he had been willing to give a loved one.

“I ain’t mad at nothing.”

TMZ reported that the order directed $929,341.50 in child and spousal support and another $150,000 to Dreka from catalog proceeds.

Asked when the relationship stopped working, he said people could take different paths and reconnect if that was meant to happen.

Earlier, Gates said he valued marriage and liked being a good husband. He entered relationships hoping they would work rather than fail.

He also said he tried to keep loved ones out of public discussion when asked about confusion over his marital status.

Gates had previously disputed whether their marriage was legally recognized. He said they held an Islamic ceremony but never completed the legal paperwork needed to make the marriage official. The two had presented themselves as husband and wife for years before he challenged that status.

Dreka filed for divorce in Los Angeles on July 30, 2025, citing irreconcilable differences, according to People, which obtained her petition. She listed July 10, 2025 as their separation date. The filing placed their wedding in October 2015.

Her petition asked for joint legal and physical custody of their children, Islah and Khaza. She also sought spousal support and payment of her attorney fees, putting both parenting arrangements and financial support before the court.

AllHipHop previously reported that Dreka sought $73,467 a month in support. That request broke down into $46,274 for spousal support and $27,193 for child support.

The split also involved a working partnership. As AllHipHop previously reported, Dreka had played a role in Gates’ career and business operations during their relationship.

Elsewhere in the interview, Gates described learning that being a provider meant more than buying things. He said his children cared about making cardboard forts with him and taught him that time together mattered more than toys.

item.title: Ye Brings Playboi Carti & North West To Houston Halloween Show
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Ye brought Playboi Carti and North West to his Houston Halloween show, pairing guest appearances with songs from across his catalog.
item.content:encoded:
Ye brought Playboi Carti and his daughter North West to his Halloween concert at Houston’s Reliant Stadium on October 31, with guest appearances woven into a set that reached across his catalog.

Carti came out alongside Ye for “Carnival” and “Off The Grid.” The guest stretch also included “Sky,” “Timeless,” “EVIL J0RDAN” and “FE!N,” giving Carti room beyond his collaborations with the night’s headliner.

North’s appearance included a remix of “Legacy,” an unnamed unreleased song and “Talking,” and Ye performed staples such as “Jesus Walks,” “All Falls Down” and “Through The Wire,” along with later selections “Ghost Town,” “Come To Life,” and “Runaway.”

The Halloween performance followed the Houston and Dallas stadium dates announced in September. For Houston, the show also marked a return after a long gap between traditional concerts in the city, since his last traditional Houston concert had been in 2013.

His more recent local appearances came in 2019, including Sunday Service at Lakewood Church and a Harris County Jail event.

Ahead of the show, the Houston Chronicle reported that Reliant Park had warned fans in a Friday, October 30 Instagram post that “outward expressions of hate will not be tolerated,” including hate symbols on clothing or signs.

The venue said it would deny entry to fans who broke those rules. The newspaper reported that it also prohibited face paint for security reasons.

The warning followed Ye’s antisemitic remarks and praise for Adolf Hitler.

Ye’s tour site lists AT&T Stadium in the Dallas area for November 7, followed by State Farm Stadium in the Phoenix area on November 21.

item.title: Lil Baby Reveals He Considered Quitting Rap While Depressed
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Lil Baby revealed he considered quitting rap while depressed as he discussed his personal struggles and new music plans.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Baby considered quitting rap while dealing with depression, a struggle he discussed in a newly released clip from his interview with The New York Times’ “Popcast”.

The Atlanta rapper also described finding his way forward after weighing an exit from music. His account came ahead of FRESH, his next album, which is due November 6.

He had spoken about the strain of fame before. In a 2022 appearance on “The Experience,” Lil Baby told host Big Loon about a long stretch of unhappiness as he adjusted to success, according to NME’s account of the interview. He said he had to change old habits, reconsider who he spent time with and rethink the way he approached his life.

On “Popcast,” he again discussed how fame could narrow a person’s world, according to the Times’ episode description. He also spoke about working beyond his usual circle of local producers as he planned his next music.

One of those new connections was with Pharrell Williams. The two worked on “Dead Fresh,” which Lil Baby first played at Louis Vuitton’s men’s show in Paris in June. The song came out in July, and his label described it as their first collaboration.

He also expressed interest in taking his music further into pop. Billboard reported that he was open to working with Sabrina Carpenter as he looked to move beyond his comfort zone.

Lil Baby drew a line between his public career and private disagreements, too. When host Joe Coscarelli asked about Young Thug and Gunna, he explained that he preferred to keep disputes between artists out of public view, according to iHeart’s account of the conversation.

“We can handle our problem off the internet, in person, just us,” he said.

He argued that public feuds reflected badly on Atlanta as a whole, no matter who appeared to win.

Young Thug is also listed alongside Future and Rylo Rodriguez on “All My Partnas,” one of the songs announced for FRESH.

His hometown is on his calendar for December 5. He had also announced the “Fresh Prince Of Atlanta” birthday concert at State Farm Arena, less than a month after the album’s planned release.

item.title: N.O.R.E. Confronts Sober Facts Over N-Word Use, Creator Responds & Questions His Approach
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: N.O.R.E. confronted food reviewer Sober Facts over his use of the N-word, and the creator challenged how he handled the dispute.
item.content:encoded:
N.O.R.E. confronted food reviewer Sober Facts in New York City over his use of the N-word, taking their months-long online argument into an encounter that drew a response from the creator.

The “Drink Champs” host approached Sober Facts while he filmed a food review. The circulating footage showed a verbal confrontation with no physical altercation.

“I could have did you filthy,” N.O.R.E. said. He maintained that his intentions were positive and argued that nobody, including Black people, should use the slur.

He addressed the camera and asked where the people backing Sober Facts online were. In a response video, Sober Facts said N.O.R.E. arrived with six or seven people and interrupted him.

“You saying to not say the N-word, and you keep saying the N-word,” he said.

The reviewer defended the word as part of New York culture.

“I’m a content demon,” he said, acknowledging he knew the clip would draw attention. He ended his response with a friendly shoutout to N.O.R.E.

N.O.R.E. and DJ EFN launched the Drink Champs Podcast Network in June 2025. It debuted with Memphis Bleek’s “Roc Solid,” with Black Effect and iHeartMedia. “Our goal is to set people up not only for success but with the tools to forge their own lanes!” the co-hosts said on Instagram.

Questions about public speech and responsibility had come up in N.O.R.E.’s own interviews earlier this year. During a June 2026 appearance on “The Breakfast Club”, he described how the fallout from his Ye interview changed the way he approached “Drink Champs.”

He said the show previously avoided editing interviews, but regretted leaving in Ye’s antisemitic remarks and comments about George Floyd. N.O.R.E. said he apologized and came to understand that hosting someone else’s words still carried a responsibility.

“I understand that I have a responsibility now,” he said. He explained that even laughing at something a guest said could make listeners think he endorsed it.

In that same June conversation, he discussed a separate online exchange with Stephen Jackson. He said internet encouragement had influenced his response, called his behavior embarrassing and expressed a preference for taking the high road.

“I want to be more responsible,” N.O.R.E. said.

item.title: Styles P Says Corporate Money Has Pulled Hip-Hop From Its Roots
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Styles P questioned Hip-Hop's corporate influence and recalled the music, mentors and basement ciphers that shaped him.
item.content:encoded:
Styles P broke down Hip-Hop’s identity crisis during an interview with TmrO Network, arguing that the genre has strayed from its foundational purpose. The LOX member traced Hip-Hop’s origins as a voice for the voiceless, a creative outlet born from poverty for people disconnected from their history, language and ancestral heritage.

He said many people no longer understood what Hip-Hop meant, pointing to the influence of media, corporations and big money.

“It’s taken away from Hip-Hop as a genre invented for people who don’t know their history, for people who didn’t know their language, for people who didn’t know their ancestors’ actual names. This is something that’s created out of poverty and out of a need to do something different. This is a generation that’s created something different to have and to hold on and to have something of your own,” Styles P said.

The Yonkers native credited early influences from Wolfman Jack’s radio presence to Lee’s style in “Beat Street” with shaping his understanding of Hip-Hop. He recalled picturing Wolfman Jack before ever seeing him. Watching Lee, meanwhile, made him want to be part of the world the film showed, from the clothes to being young and out in the mix.

He also described “The Message” as his first experience of a “verbal picture.” Its words reflected poverty and places he had seen while traveling through New York with his mother, who cleaned homes and apartment buildings. Hearing those familiar surroundings put into words helped draw him toward rap’s storytelling.

Styles P highlighted how corporate involvement had pulled attention away from Hip-Hop’s roots. For his generation, he explained, the culture gave people a voice and something of their own to build around.

“It’s like the matrix was broke,” he said. “It was like it’s something they created and it was a voice for us. … So I think a lot of us tend to forget that and forget the importance of this [ __ ].”

The LOX co-founder reflected on his journey from sneaking into basement ciphers in Yonkers to becoming a Hip-Hop veteran. He said he began rhyming around 10 or 11. He heard people on his block banging on car hoods and rhyming and already knew he loved words. He credited an older rapper, Dusty Mike from Highland, with showing him how sharp wordplay could command a room. He admired how Dusty Mike paired an aggressive style with an intelligent approach to rhymes. Around 11 or 12, he recalled getting the mic at a basement party and realizing the crowd liked what he was doing.

His future group members also helped raise his standards. Styles P said he met fellow LOX members Jadakiss and Sheek Louch in junior high before they attended high school together. Their approach pushed him beyond trading rhymes: they were already writing songs and hooks and recording on reel-to-reel equipment. Seeing that work up close made him take his own craft more seriously.

item.title: Too $hort Says Mount Westmore Pays More For A Fraction Of The Work
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Too $hort said Mount Westmore paid more for a fraction of his solo workload and explained why cultural reach mattered, too.
item.content:encoded:
Too $hort said sharing a stage with Snoop Dogg, Ice Cube and E-40 paid him more for a lot less work.

REVOLT released his “Effective Immediately” interview with DJ Hed and Gina Views on October 29. The rapper put his Mount Westmore workload at 20 to 25 percent of a solo show. He did not name a dollar amount.

“The best side hustle I’ve ever had in my life.”

He traced the group to E-40’s pandemic phone calls. Ice Cube came up with the name, and Too $hort needed little convincing to join.

His praise for the group’s earning power goes back years. In a 2022 SPIN interview, Too $hort explained that Mount Westmore brought in business without taking away his solo offers. He said the group had already earned millions before its December album release. He also saw it as proof that veteran rappers could keep building careers rather than step aside because of their age.

Ice Cube described a similar benefit in the studio during that interview. Each member only had to deliver one verse per song instead of carrying an entire album alone. That did not mean anyone could coast: Cube said a weak contribution would stand out next to the other three MCs.

Finding time for the group has been another matter. In an April interview with AllHipHop, Too $hort said the members’ busy lives made it hard to coordinate. They wanted to play shows and put out more music, but each had plenty going on outside Mount Westmore.

At that point, he said they had recorded enough material for three albums. Their talks centered on whether to release those songs as recorded or build new tracks from them. The issue was how to shape the music they already had, rather than start another round of recording from scratch.

Money was not his only measure of value in the current REVOLT conversation. Asked about protecting his signature B-word, Too $hort said requiring permission would have kept it from spreading through pop culture. Hearing it in films, television and other artists’ songs was its own reward.

He made a similar argument on “Big Facts” in 2022, describing Hip-Hop’s phrases and styles as contributions for others to use.

In the new interview, he put it this way: “Every time you run it, you just pay me.”

item.title: SNL Mocks Nicki Minaj’s Trump Support With Career Joke
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Saidah Belo-Osagie played Nicki Minaj on SNL, turning the rapper's Trump support and press secretary talk into a Halloween joke.
item.content:encoded:
“Saturday Night Live” turned Nicki Minaj‘s support for Donald Trump into a career joke on its October 31 Halloween episode, with Saidah Belo-Osagie playing the rapper.

The cold open cast Belo-Osagie’s Minaj as Trump’s next choice for press secretary.

“Trump’s out here killing it … and by it, I mean my career,” the performer joked as Minaj on SNL.

James Austin Johnson’s Trump also fixated on the Minaj character’s backside. In the sketch, he suggested he could appreciate it if it belonged to a man.

“I could admire it,” Johnson said as Trump.

The parody took place inside a haunted attraction, where a couple’s Halloween ride was interrupted by Johnson’s Trump.

Tom Hanks returned as David S. Pumpkins, the character he first played in 2016. Johnson’s Trump compared himself with Pumpkins, joking that both arrived in 2016 and were loud, orange and annoying.

The ride was called “Tombs of Doom.” Kenan Thompson served as the guide, while Veronika Slowikowska’s Katie Zacharia flubbed the show’s opening line.

For Belo-Osagie, the Minaj impression came early in her time on the show.

The New York comedian joined Grace Reiter as a new featured player for Season 52, which premiered September 26. Her background includes character comedy and “UNSCRIPTED,” a reality-TV parody variety show at Brooklyn’s Union Hall.

The press secretary bit followed Trump’s own remarks in a recent Benny Johnson interview. Trump liked the idea of Minaj taking the job.

“That’s a good idea. I think I’ll have to think about that,” Trump said on Johnson’s show. He mentioned Johnson as another choice. He did not offer Minaj the job or appoint her.

The chatter followed an October 25 Air Force One video shared by White House communications director Steven Cheung.

In his caption, Cheung suggested Minaj for the job. The rapper praised Trump’s business background and his recovery from money trouble. She also praised his stamina. Their discussion covered the economy, polls and Trump’s campaign workload.

Minaj also urged people to vote for Republicans in the November 3 midterms.

She made the appeal at an October 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan. She pledged to back Trump if he ran again.
